title: Subsets
problem: Given an array nums of unique integers, return all possible subsets (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets, and it can be in any order.
example: Explanation: 3 elements, each either in or out, gives 2^3 = 8 subsets.
intuition: Every element faces exactly one yes/no decision: is it in the subset or not? Line those decisions up one after another and you get a binary tree of depth n whose 2^n leaves are exactly the subsets. That tree is the whole problem.
A neat way to see the same thing without recursion: number the subsets 0.. 2^n - 1. The binary digits of the number tell you which elements are in. 5 = 101 means take nums[0] and nums[2].
The backtracking version is the one interviewers want to see, because the same code shape (add, recurse, remove) is reused all day.
notes: Say it like this: "Each element is either in or out, so there are 2^n subsets. I can enumerate bitmasks from 0 to 2^n − 1 in O(n·2^n), or do backtracking where every recursion node records the current path and loops forward from start. Both are O(n·2^n), which is optimal since that is the output size; backtracking generalises to the harder variants."
Edge cases: empty array (answer is [[]]), single element.
Common mistakes: adding path itself instead of a copy (all entries end up empty); forgetting to pop after recursion; looping from 0 instead of start (creates duplicates/permutations).
Follow-ups: "What if there are duplicates?" → Subsets II (sort + skip same value at the same level). "Iterative?" → start with [[]]; for each number, append it to a copy of every existing subset. 9.2
simple: List every subset of the numbers.

approaches.label: Brute Force (bitmask enumeration)
steps: Loop mask from 0 to 2^n - 1.
For each mask, check every bit i; if bit i is set, add nums[i].
Add the built list to the answer.
approaches.why: There are 2^n masks and each one is scanned bit by bit in O(n); only the current list is extra memory.
approaches.simple: Count from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1; the 1-bits in each count say which numbers to include.

approaches.label: Optimal (backtracking)
steps: dfs(start): the current path is itself a valid subset, so record a copy.
For every index i from start to n-1: add nums[i], call dfs(i+1), then remove it.
Starting at i+1 guarantees each subset is built in increasing index order, so no duplicates.
approaches.why: There are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to O(n); this is optimal because the output itself has that size.
approaches.simple: Backtracking: record the current picks, then try adding each later number, go deeper, and remove it again.

title: Combination Sum
problem: Given an array of distinct positive integers candidates and a target, return all unique combinations where the chosen numbers sum to target. The same number may be used unlimited times. Two combinations are the same if they use the same numbers with the same frequencies.
example: Explanation: 2+2+3 = 7 and 7 = 7. No other multiset works.
intuition: It is Subsets with two twists: you can reuse an element, and you only keep paths whose sum hits the target. To allow reuse, after choosing candidates[i] you recurse with the same i instead of i+1. To avoid getting [2,3,2] and [3,2,2] as separate answers, you still never go backwards: index i only lets you pick from i onwards.

Pruning is the speed-up: all numbers are positive, so once the remaining target goes negative there is no point going deeper. If you sort the candidates first, you can even break the loop the moment candidates[i] > remaining, because every later number is bigger too.
notes: Say it like this: "It is backtracking where after picking a number I recurse on the same index so it can be reused, and I never move backwards so each multiset appears once. Sorting lets me break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target. Worst case is exponential, about 2^(target/min), which is unavoidable since the output can be that large."
Edge cases: no combination exists (return empty list); target smaller than every candidate; a candidate equal to target.
Common mistakes: recursing with i+1 (forbids reuse) or with 0 (creates permutations like [2,3,2] and [3,2,2]); using sort() without a comparator in JS (sorts as strings).
Follow-ups: "Only count the combinations?" → unbounded knapsack DP: dp[s] += dp[s - c] with coins in the outer loop, O(n · target). "Each number used once?" → Combination Sum II. 9.3
simple: Find every combination (numbers can repeat) that adds up to the target.

approaches.label: Brute Force (pick / not-pick on each index)
steps: dfs(i, remaining): if remaining == 0, record the path. If i == n or remaining < 0, return.
Option A: pick candidates[i] and stay at i (so it can be picked again).
Option B: skip to i+1.
approaches.time: O(2^t) roughly, where t = target / min(candidate)
approaches.why: Each level makes two choices and the deepest chain is when you keep picking the smallest number t times. No pruning beyond remaining < 0.
approaches.simple: For each number, either take it (and stay on it) or skip to the next one.

approaches.label: Optimal (sorted loop-style backtracking with early break)
steps: Sort candidates.
dfs(start, remaining): if remaining == 0, record the path.
Loop i from start: if candidates[i] > remaining, break (all later ones are larger). Otherwise choose it, recurse with dfs(i, remaining - candidates[i]), un-choose.
approaches.time: O(2^t) worst case, much faster in practice
approaches.why: The worst-case tree size is the same exponential, but sorting lets us cut whole branches the moment a number is too big; depth is bounded by target / smallest candidate.
approaches.simple: Sort, then loop over choices; once a number is too big, all later ones are too, so stop early.

title: Combination Sum II
problem: Given candidates (which may contain duplicates) and a target, return all unique combinations that sum to target. Each element may be used at most once, and the answer must not contain duplicate combinations.
example: Explanation: The two 1s may both be used in one combination, but [1,7] must appear only once.
intuition: Two changes from Combination Sum: use each index once (recurse with i+1), and the input has duplicates. If you treat the two 1 s as different, you will produce [1,7] twice (once with each 1).

The fix is the most important trick of the day: sort, then at the same level of the tree, skip a value equal to the one just tried. In the loop for i in start..n-1, the condition i > start && c[i] == c[i-1] means "I already started a branch with this value at this position; a second branch would produce the same combinations". Note it is i > start, not i > 0: going deeper and picking the second 1 right after the first 1 is allowed, which is how [1,1,6] is formed.
notes: Say it like this: "The brute force generates every subset summing to target and dedupes with a set, which wastes work and memory. Instead I sort and, inside the loop at each recursion level, skip a value equal to the previous one, so each distinct combination is built exactly once. I also break early once a value exceeds the remaining target. Worst case is still O(n·2^n) but with no duplicate exploration."
Edge cases: all elements equal (e.g. [1,1,1,1], target 2 gives one answer [1,1]); no answer.
Common mistakes: writing i > 0 instead of i > start (this wrongly forbids [1,1,6]); forgetting to sort; recursing with i instead of i+1.

Follow-ups: "Why i > start?" → The skip is only about siblings in the same loop; a child is allowed to take the next equal value. "Combination Sum III (k numbers from 1–9)?" → same template with a size limit. 9.4
simple: Like Combination Sum, but each number can be used once and answers must not repeat.

approaches.label: Brute Force (generate all, deduplicate with a set)
steps: Sort the array so equal combinations look identical as lists.
Pick / not-pick every index (each used once), collecting paths that sum to target.
Put them in a Set to drop duplicates.
approaches.space: O(n · 2^n) for the set in the worst case
approaches.why: Every subset may be explored and each recorded path costs O(n) to copy and hash; the set may hold many lists.
approaches.simple: Generate all combinations and remove duplicates with a set.

approaches.label: Optimal (sort + skip duplicates at the same level)
steps: Sort candidates.
dfs(start, remaining): if remaining == 0, record.
Loop i from start: if i > start && c[i] == c[i-1], continue (duplicate branch). If c[i] > remaining, break. Otherwise choose, dfs(i+1, remaining - c[i]), un-choose.
approaches.why: Still exponential in the worst case, but no duplicate branch is ever explored and no set is needed.
approaches.simple: Sort, and at each level skip a number equal to the one just tried, so the same combination is never built twice.

title: Permutations
problem: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible permutations in any order.
intuition: In Subsets the question at each step was "take or skip". In Permutations the question is "which unused element goes in the next slot?" Slot 1 has n options, slot 2 has n-1, and so on, giving n! leaves. Because order matters now, the loop always runs from 0, not from start; you just skip elements already in the path.

Two common ways to track "unused": a boolean[] used array, or swapping elements in place so the prefix nums[0..k-1] is the fixed part and nums[k..] are the unused candidates. Swapping avoids the extra array.
notes: Say it like this: "Each slot picks one of the remaining elements, so there are n! permutations. A naive version checks path.contains in O(n) per step; I avoid that by swapping so the unused elements are always the suffix nums[k..]. That gives O(n·n!) time, which matches the output size, and O(n) recursion space."
Edge cases: single element; empty array returns [[]].
Common mistakes: forgetting to swap back; using start like Subsets (that gives combinations, not permutations).
Follow-ups: "Duplicates in input?" (Permutations II) → sort, use used[], and skip nums[i] if nums[i] == nums[i-1] &&!used[i-1]. "Next permutation only?" → O(n) find-pivot, swap, reverse suffix. 9.5
simple: List every ordering of the numbers.

approaches.label: Brute Force (path + contains check)
steps: Build a path. At each step loop over all elements.
Skip an element if path already contains it (linear search).
When path.size() == n, record a copy.
approaches.why: There are about n·n! recursion steps, and each contains check costs O(n) more.
approaches.simple: Build the order one position at a time, skipping numbers already used.

approaches.label: Optimal (in-place swapping)
steps: dfs(k): positions 0..k-1 are fixed. If k == n, record the array.
For i from k to n-1: swap nums[k] and nums[i] (put candidate i in slot k), recurse dfs(k+1), swap back.
approaches.why: There are n! permutations and copying each costs O(n); the "is it used?" check is O(1) because the unused elements are exactly nums[k..].
approaches.simple: Swap each candidate into the current position, recurse, and swap it back.

title: Subsets II
problem: Given an integer array nums that may contain duplicates, return all possible subsets without duplicate subsets, in any order.
example: Explanation: [1,2] would appear twice if the two 2s were treated as different; it must appear once.
intuition: This is Subsets (9.1) plus the duplicate rule from Combination Sum II (9.3). Sort so equal values sit together. Then, inside the loop at one recursion level, start a branch only for the first occurrence of each value: if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;.

Why it works: at a given level, choosing the first 2 or the second 2 leads to identical sets of subsets underneath. Going deeper, the first 2 can still be followed by the second 2 (since that happens at the next level, where i == start), which is how [1,2,2] is formed.
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force generates all 2^n subsets of the sorted array and dedupes with a set. Better: sort and, in the backtracking loop, only branch on the first occurrence of each value at a given level, so duplicates are never created. Time is O(n·2^n), space O(n) apart from the output."
Edge cases: all elements equal ([2,2,2] gives [],[2],[2,2],[2,2,2]); no duplicates (behaves like Subsets).
Common mistakes: not sorting; using i > 0 instead of i > start.
Follow-ups: "Without recursion?" → iterative: when the current number equals the previous one, only extend the subsets added in the previous round. 9.6
simple: List every subset when the numbers can repeat, without duplicate subsets.

approaches.label: Brute Force (all subsets + set)
steps: Sort nums.
Generate all 2^n subsets (as in 9.1).
Store them in a Set so equal lists collapse into one.
approaches.why: All 2^n subsets are generated and each costs O(n) to copy and hash; the set stores them all.
approaches.simple: Make all subsets and remove duplicates with a set.

approaches.label: Optimal (sort + skip at the same level)
steps: Sort nums.
dfs(start): record a copy of path.
Loop i from start: skip if i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]; else choose, dfs(i+1), un-choose.
approaches.why: At most 2^n distinct subsets are produced, each copied in O(n); no duplicate is ever generated so no set is needed.
approaches.simple: Sort, then in the backtracking loop skip a number equal to the previous one at the same level.

title: Generate Parentheses
problem: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses.
example: Explanation: These are the 5 balanced strings of length 6 (the 3rd Catalan number).
intuition: Build the string one character at a time. You do not need to generate garbage and filter it: just never make an illegal move. Two rules are enough: - You may add (if you have used fewer than n opens. - You may add) only if close < open (there is an unmatched (waiting).
If you follow these rules, every string of length 2n you reach is automatically valid. The count of results is the Catalan number C(n) ≈ 4^n / (n√n).
notes: Say it like this: "Brute force generates all 2^(2n) strings and validates each in O(n). Instead I backtrack and only add '(' while open < n and ')' while close < open, so every completed string is valid by construction. The work is proportional to the Catalan number, about 4^n/√n."
Edge cases: n = 1 gives ["()"].
Common mistakes: allowing) when close <= open (should be strictly less); using string concatenation in Java everywhere (works but allocates; StringBuilder with undo is cleaner).
Follow-ups: "Just the count?" → Catalan number, DP C(n) = sum C(i)·C(n-1-i). "Validate a string?" → counter or stack. 9.7
simple: List every valid arrangement of n pairs of brackets.

approaches.label: Brute Force (all 2^(2n) strings, then validate)
steps: Generate every string of length 2n over {'(', ')'}.
For each full string, check balance with a counter (never negative, ends at 0).
Keep the valid ones.
approaches.why: There are 2^(2n) strings, each validated in O(n).
approaches.simple: Make every string of ( and ) of length 2n and keep the balanced ones.

approaches.label: Optimal (backtracking with open/close counts)
steps: dfs(open, close): if length is 2n, record.
If open < n: add (, recurse, remove.
If close < open: add), recurse, remove.
approaches.why: We only ever visit prefixes of valid strings; the number of valid results is the Catalan number ~4^n/(n√n), each built in O(n).
approaches.simple: Only add ( if you still have some left, and only add ) if it closes an open one.

title: Word Search
problem: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word can be formed by a path of sequentially adjacent cells (up/down/left/right). The same cell may not be used more than once in a path.
intuition: Try every cell as a starting point. From a cell matching word[k], try the 4 neighbours for word[k+1]. That is DFS. The backtracking part is the "no reuse" rule: while a cell is on the current path it must be blocked, and once we return from it, it must be unblocked so other paths can use it.
The cleanest trick is to temporarily overwrite the cell with a marker like '#' (so it cannot match any letter), recurse, then restore the original letter. That replaces a separate visited array.
notes: Say it like this: "I start a DFS from every cell, matching one character per step and marking the cell as used by overwriting it with '#', then restoring it on the way back. That is O(m·n·3^L) time and O(L) stack. I add cheap pruning: a letter-count check and starting from the rarer end of the word."
Edge cases: single-cell board; word longer than the board; word using the same letter more times than the board has.
Common mistakes: forgetting to restore the cell (breaks later searches); returning early without restoring; checking bounds after accessing the array.
Follow-ups: "Many words?" → Word Search II: build a Trie of words and DFS once from each cell, walking the Trie instead of a single word. 9.8
simple: Can the word be traced on the grid by moving up, down, left or right without reusing a cell?

approaches.label: Brute Force (DFS with a visited matrix)
steps: For every cell, start dfs(r, c, 0).
dfs fails if out of bounds, already visited, or letter mismatch; succeeds if k == word.length - 1 and it matches.
Mark visited[r][c], try 4 neighbours, unmark.
approaches.space: O(m · n) for visited + O(L) recursion
approaches.why: Each of m·n starts can branch 4 ways for up to L levels; visited costs a full grid.
approaches.simple: From every cell, explore with a visited grid.

approaches.label: Optimal (in-place marking + pruning)
steps: Quick prune: if word is longer than m·n, or the board lacks enough of some letter, return false.
(Optional heuristic) If the last letter of word is rarer on the board than the first, reverse word so the search starts from the rarer end and dies sooner.
DFS as before, but mark a cell by setting it to '#' and restore it afterwards.
approaches.why: After the first step, a path never goes back to the cell it came from, so each step has at most 3 new directions; no visited array is needed.
approaches.simple: Same search, but mark cells in place and quit early if the board lacks enough letters.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
pattern: Backtracking on cut positions, DP precompute
problem: Given a string s, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome. Return all possible such partitions.
example: Explanation: "aab" can be cut as a|a|b or aa|b; "aab" and "ab" are not palindromes.
intuition: Think of it as deciding where the first piece ends. From position start, try every end i; if s[start..i] is a palindrome, take it as the next piece and recursively partition the rest s[i+1..]. When start reaches the end of the string, the current list of pieces is a full answer.

The only repeated work is the palindrome check. Checking s[start..i] with two pointers each time costs O(n). We can precompute a table pal[i][j] in O(n²) so each check is O(1): pal[i][j] = s[i]==s[j] && (j - i < 2 || pal[i+1][j-1]).
notes: Say it like this: "I backtrack on where the next piece ends: from start I try every end and recurse only if s[start..end] is a palindrome. That is O(n·2^n) because of up to 2^(n-1) partitions. To avoid re-checking palindromes I precompute an O(n²) table so each check is O(1)."
Edge cases: single character; all same characters (maximum number of partitions); no repeated characters (only one partition, all single letters).
Common mistakes: filling the DP table in the wrong order (i must go downwards); off-by-one in substring(start, end + 1).
Follow-ups: "Minimum cuts?" (Palindrome Partitioning II) → DP: cuts[i] = min(cuts[j-1] + 1) over palindromic s[j..i], O(n²). 9.9
simple: Split the string into pieces that are all palindromes; list every way.

approaches.label: Brute Force (backtracking with two-pointer check)
steps: dfs(start): if start == n, record the path.
For each end from start to n-1: if isPal(start, end) (two pointers), add the substring, dfs(end+1), remove.
approaches.why: There are up to 2^(n-1) ways to cut the string, and each piece costs O(n) to check and copy.
approaches.simple: Backtracking: try every first piece that is a palindrome, then split the rest.

approaches.label: Optimal (precomputed palindrome table + backtracking)
steps: Fill pal[i][j] for all i <= j, iterating i from n-1 down to 0 so pal[i+1][j-1] is ready.
Backtrack exactly as before, but check pal[start][end] in O(1).
approaches.why: The output itself can be O(n·2^n) (e.g. "aaaa…"), so this is optimal; the table removes the repeated O(n) checks at a cost of O(n²) memory.
approaches.simple: Same backtracking, but first build a table that tells instantly whether any piece is a palindrome.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problem: Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return all possible letter combinations the number could represent using the old phone keypad mapping (2 = abc, 3 = def, …, 7 = pqrs, 9 = wxyz). Return an empty list if the input is empty.
example: Explanation: 3 letters for '2' times 3 letters for '3' = 9 strings.
intuition: This is a pure Cartesian product: position k of the answer string is any letter mapped from digits[k]. The recursion tree has depth = number of digits and branching factor 3 or 4. There is nothing to prune; every leaf is an answer.

You can do it recursively (backtracking with a StringBuilder) or iteratively (start with [""], and for each digit, extend every existing string with each of its letters). Both are optimal, since the output itself is O(4^n) strings of length n.
notes: Say it like this: "It is a Cartesian product of the letter groups, so the output has up to 4^n strings. I backtrack position by position with a single StringBuilder, which is O(n·4^n) time and O(n) extra space; an iterative expansion has the same time but keeps intermediate lists."
Edge cases: empty input must return [], not [""]; digits 7 and 9 have 4 letters.
Common mistakes: returning [""] for empty input; mapping off by two (index the array by digit value, keeping 0 and 1 empty).
Follow-ups: "Digits 0/1 present?" → they map to nothing; either skip them or return empty depending on the spec. 9.10
simple: List all letter combinations a phone number could spell.

approaches.label: Brute Force (iterative BFS-style expansion)
steps: Start res = [""].
For each digit, build a new list: for every string in res and every letter of the digit, append str + letter.
Replace res with the new list.
approaches.why: Each round creates new strings for every partial result; intermediate lists are kept in memory.
approaches.simple: Start with an empty string and, for each digit, extend every string with every letter.

approaches.label: Optimal (backtracking with a shared buffer)
steps: dfs(k): if k == digits.length, record the buffer as a string.
For each letter of digits[k]: append it, dfs(k+1), remove it.
approaches.why: There are up to 4^n leaves and building each string is O(n); only one buffer of length n is used for partial work.
approaches.simple: Backtracking: choose a letter for the current digit, go to the next digit, then undo.

title: N Queens
problem: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (same row, column or diagonal). Return all distinct board configurations, each as a list of strings where 'Q' is a queen and '.' is empty.
example: Explanation: There are exactly two solutions for a 4x4 board.
intuition: Every row must hold exactly one queen, so place queens row by row: the choice at row r is which column to use. That instantly removes row conflicts and shrinks the search from "any n cells out of n²" to n^n, and pruning cuts it to roughly n!.

For a candidate cell (r, c) we need to know if its column or either diagonal is already taken. Cells on the same "\" diagonal share r - c; cells on the same "/" diagonal share r + c. Keep three boolean arrays: cols[c], diag1[r - c + n - 1], diag2[r + c]. Then the safety check is O(1) instead of scanning the board.
notes: Say it like this: "I place one queen per row, so I only choose a column at each level. The naive check scans the column and diagonals in O(n); I make it O(1) with three boolean arrays indexed by column, r−c, and r+c. The search is about O(n!) with O(n) extra space plus the board for output."
Edge cases: n = 1 → [["Q"]]; n = 2 and n = 3 → no solutions (empty list).
Common mistakes: negative index for r - c (add n - 1); forgetting to unmark the diagonals; mixing up which diagonal uses sum vs difference.
Follow-ups: "Only count solutions?" (N-Queens II) → same DFS, increment a counter; can use bitmasks for columns/diagonals for speed: avail = ~(cols | d1 | d2) & ((1<<n)-1). 9.11
simple: Place n queens on an n×n board so none attack each other. List every way.

approaches.label: Brute Force (row-by-row, scan the board to check safety)
steps: dfs(r): if r == n, record the board.
For each column c: check the column above and both upward diagonals by scanning the board (O(n)).
If safe: place 'Q', dfs(r+1), remove.
approaches.why: Pruning leaves about n! partial placements, and each safety check scans up to O(n) cells.
approaches.simple: Place one queen per row, checking the board above for column and diagonal clashes.

approaches.label: Optimal (O(1) conflict check with column/diagonal arrays)
steps: Keep cols[n], diag1[2n-1] (index r - c + n - 1), diag2[2n-1] (index r + c).
dfs(r): for each c, skip if any of the three is taken; else mark all three, place 'Q', dfs(r+1), unmark.
approaches.space: O(n²) for the board (O(n) for the sets)
approaches.why: Same search tree, but each safety check is O(1); the board is needed only to build the output strings.
approaches.simple: Keep arrays that remember which columns and diagonals are taken, so each check is instant.

title: Sudoku Solver
problem: Fill the empty cells ('.') of a 9x9 Sudoku board in place so that every row, every column and every 3x3 box contains the digits 1 – 9 exactly once. The input is guaranteed to have exactly one solution.
example: Explanation: Each row, column and 3x3 box now has 1-9 once.
intuition: Find an empty cell, try digits 1 – 9, place one that does not conflict, and recurse to the next empty cell. If later you get stuck (a cell where no digit fits), return false so the caller erases its digit and tries the next one. The first time you reach "no empty cells left", you are done, and you propagate true all the way up so nothing gets erased.

The box index for cell (r, c) is (r / 3) * 3 + c / 3. Instead of scanning the row, column and box every time (27 cells), keep three tables row[9][10], col[9][10], box[9][10] of "digit used" flags so each check is O(1).
notes: Say it like this: "I backtrack over empty cells, trying digits 1–9 and recursing; if a cell has no valid digit I return false so the caller undoes its choice. The basic version scans 27 cells to validate; I keep row, column and box used-digit tables so each check is O(1). Worst case is O(9^m) for m empty cells, but the constraints prune massively; picking the most-constrained cell first is a further heuristic."
Edge cases: board already full (return immediately); the input is guaranteed solvable, so no need to report failure.

Common mistakes: not returning true up the stack (the board gets erased while unwinding); wrong box index formula; forgetting to return false after trying all 9 digits in the scan version (it would continue to the next cell and skip this one).
Follow-ups: "Validate a Sudoku (Valid Sudoku)?" → one pass with the same three tables. "Make it faster?" → bitmasks per row/col/box and choose the cell with the fewest candidates (MRV). 9.12
simple: Fill in a Sudoku.

approaches.label: Brute Force (backtracking with a scan-based validity check)
steps: Scan for the first '.'. If none, return true.
For d in '1'..'9': if isValid(r, c, d) (scan row, column, box), place it and recurse. If recursion returns true, return true; else reset to '.'.
If no digit worked, return false.
approaches.why: Each empty cell can try up to 9 digits, and each validity check scans 27 cells. In practice the constraints prune heavily.
approaches.simple: Find an empty cell, try digits 1–9 that don't clash, recurse, and undo if stuck.

approaches.label: Optimal (precomputed used-digit tables + list of empty cells)
steps: Pre-fill rowUsed[9][10], colUsed[9][10], boxUsed[9][10] from the given digits, and collect all empty cells into a list.
dfs(idx): if idx == empties.size(), return true. Take cell (r, c) = empties[idx], box b.
For d in 1..9 not used in row/col/box: mark all three, write it, recurse dfs(idx+1); on false, unmark and erase.
approaches.why: Each check is now O(1) and we never rescan for the next empty cell. (A further real-world speed-up is to always pick the empty cell with the fewest options, but it does not change the worst-case bound.)
approaches.simple: Same backtracking, with tables of used digits per row, column and box so checks are instant.

title: Rotate Image
problem: Given an n x n matrix representing an image, rotate it by 90 degrees clockwise, in place (do not allocate another matrix).
example: Explanation: The first column read bottom-up (7,4,1) becomes the first row.
intuition: Look at where one cell goes: after a clockwise rotation, element (i, j) lands at (j, n-1-i). That mapping is two simple moves glued together: 1. Transpose (swap across the main diagonal): (i, j) → (j, i). 2. Reverse each row: (j, i) → (j, n-1-i).
Both moves are easy to do in place with swaps, so the whole rotation is in place. (Counter-clockwise would be transpose + reverse each column.)
notes: Say it like this: "Cell (i, j) moves to (j, n−1−i). Copying into a new matrix is O(n²) time and space. In place, I transpose and then reverse every row, which composes to exactly that mapping, in O(n²) time and O(1) space."
Edge cases: 1x1 matrix; even vs odd n (both work with this method).
Common mistakes: transposing with j starting at 0 (every pair is swapped twice, nothing changes); reversing columns instead of rows (gives counter-clockwise).
Follow-ups: "Counter-clockwise?" → transpose + reverse columns (or reverse rows first, then transpose). "Alternative?" → rotate layer by layer, moving 4 cells at a time in a cycle. 9.13
simple: Rotate a square matrix 90° clockwise.

approaches.label: Brute Force (copy into a new matrix)
steps: Create res[n][n].
For each (i, j): res[j][n-1-i] = matrix[i][j].
Copy res back into matrix.
approaches.why: Every cell is moved once, but a full second matrix is used, which breaks the in-place requirement.
approaches.simple: Copy each value to its rotated spot in a new matrix.

approaches.label: Optimal (transpose, then reverse each row)
steps: For i < j, swap matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i] (transpose).
For each row, reverse it with two pointers.
approaches.why: Each cell is touched a constant number of times, and only a temporary variable is used.
approaches.simple: Flip the matrix over its diagonal, then reverse each row. Done in place.

title: Spiral Matrix
problem: Given an m x n matrix, return all its elements in spiral order (start top-left, go right, then down, then left, then up, and keep spiralling inwards).
example: Explanation: Outer ring clockwise, then the inner row 6,7.
intuition: Keep four walls: top, bottom, left, right. Walk the top row left→right, then move top down. Walk the right column top→bottom, then move right left. Walk the bottom row right→left (only if top <= bottom still), then move bottom up. Walk the left column bottom→top (only if left <= right still), then move left right. Repeat while the walls haven't crossed.
The two "only if" checks are the whole difficulty: for a single remaining row or column, without them you would read it twice.
notes: Say it like this: "A simulation with direction vectors and a visited grid works in O(m·n) time and space. I instead keep four boundaries and peel one ring at a time, shrinking a boundary after each side, with checks so a single leftover row or column isn't read twice. That's O(m·n) time and O(1) extra space."
Edge cases: single row; single column; 1x1; non-square matrices.
Common mistakes: missing the top <= bottom / left <= right checks (duplicates in the middle row/column).
Follow-ups: "Spiral Matrix II (fill 1..n² in spiral)?" → same boundaries, write instead of read. 9.14
simple: Read a matrix in a spiral, clockwise from the top-left.

approaches.label: Brute Force (simulate with direction vectors + visited)
steps: Keep visited[m][n] and a direction index over right, down, left, up.
Take m·n steps: record the cell, mark it, and if the next cell is out of bounds or visited, turn clockwise.
approaches.why: Each cell is visited once, but the visited matrix costs extra memory.
approaches.simple: Walk and turn right whenever you hit an edge or a visited cell.

steps: top = 0, bottom = m-1, left = 0, right = n-1.
While top <= bottom && left <= right: top row, top++; right column, right--; if top <= bottom bottom row reversed, bottom--; if left <= right left column upwards, left++.
approaches.why: Each element is emitted exactly once and only four integers track state.
approaches.simple: Keep four borders (top, bottom, left, right) and peel one layer at a time, moving the border inward.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problem: Given an m x n integer matrix, if an element is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Do it in place.
example: Explanation: The 0 at (1,1) wipes row 1 and column 1.
intuition: The trap: if you zero out rows and columns while scanning, new zeros you just wrote look like original zeros and wipe everything. So separate the marking phase from the writing phase.

Marking needs to remember "which rows and which columns contain a zero". Two arrays row[m] and col[n] do it in O(m + n). To get O(1) space, reuse the matrix itself: the first row stores column flags and the first column stores row flags. Cell (0,0) would be shared by both, so keep one extra variable col0 for the first column.
notes: Say it like this: "I must separate marking from writing, or new zeros cascade. With row and column boolean arrays it's O(m·n) time and O(m+n) space. For O(1) space I store the flags in the first row and first column, with one extra variable for column 0 since cell (0,0) can only hold one flag, and I process the inner cells before the first row and column."
Edge cases: zero in the first row or first column; single row/column; no zeros at all.
Common mistakes: zeroing during the first scan; processing row 0 / column 0 before the inner cells (destroys flags); using matrix[0][0] for both the first row and first column.
Follow-ups: "Why not mark with a sentinel like -1?" → values can be any integer, so a sentinel isn't safe. 9.15
simple: If a cell is 0, make its whole row and column 0.

approaches.label: Brute Force (copy the matrix)
steps: Copy the matrix.
For every zero in the copy, zero its row and column in the original.
approaches.why: For each zero (up to m·n of them) we write a whole row and column; the copy keeps original zeros distinguishable.
approaches.simple: Copy the matrix and use the copy to know where the original zeros were.

approaches.label: Better (row and column flag arrays)
steps: Pass 1: for every zero at (i, j), set row[i] = true, col[j] = true.
Pass 2: set matrix[i][j] = 0 if row[i] || col[j].
approaches.why: Two passes over the grid; the flags need one entry per row and per column.
approaches.simple: Remember which rows and columns contain a zero, then clear them.

approaches.label: Optimal (first row and column as flags)
steps: Use matrix[i][0] as the flag for row i and matrix[0][j] as the flag for column j (for j >= 1). Use a variable col0 for column 0.
Pass 1: for every zero at (i, j): set matrix[i][0] = 0; if j == 0 set col0 = true, else matrix[0][j] = 0.
Pass 2: for i >= 1, j >= 1, zero the cell if its row flag or column flag is 0.
Then handle row 0 (if matrix[0][0] == 0, zero the whole first row), and finally column 0 (if col0, zero the whole first column). Order matters: the flags must be read before they are overwritten.
approaches.why: Still two passes, but the flags live inside the matrix itself.
approaches.simple: Use the first row and first column of the matrix itself as the memory, with one extra flag for column 0.

title: Happy Number
problem: A number is happy if repeatedly replacing it with the sum of the squares of its digits eventually reaches 1. If it loops forever in a cycle that does not include 1, it is not happy. Return whether n is happy.
intuition: The sequence of numbers is like a linked list where next(x) = sumOfDigitSquares(x). Numbers shrink fast (a 3- digit number maps to at most 243), so the sequence must eventually either hit 1 or repeat. "Does it repeat?" is cycle detection: either remember what you've seen in a set, or use Floyd's slow/fast pointers with O(1) memory, exactly like Linked List Cycle.
notes: Say it like this: "The digit-square map turns this into a linked list that either reaches 1 or cycles. A hash set of seen values detects the cycle; Floyd's tortoise and hare does it in O(1) space. Both are effectively O(log n) since values drop below a few hundred after one step."
Edge cases: n = 1 (true immediately); n = 7 (happy); unhappy numbers all fall into the cycle 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4.
Common mistakes: infinite loop with no cycle detection; integer division in JS without Math.floor.
Follow-ups: "Why must it terminate?" → for n ≥ 1000 the next value has fewer digits; below 1000 it's at most 243, so values are bounded and must repeat. 9.16
simple: Keep replacing a number by the sum of the squares of its digits. Does it reach 1?

approaches.label: Brute Force (hash set of seen numbers)
steps: While n!= 1 and n not in seen: add n, replace n with its digit-square sum.
Return n == 1.
approaches.why: Each step costs O(digits) and after the first step values stay below ~243, so only a bounded number of distinct values appear.
approaches.simple: Remember numbers you have seen; repeating one means you are stuck in a loop.

approaches.label: Optimal (Floyd's slow/fast pointers)
steps: slow = n, fast = next(n).
While fast!= 1 && slow!= fast: slow = next(slow), fast = next(next(fast)).
Return fast == 1.
approaches.why: Same number of steps up to a constant; the fast pointer meets the slow one inside any cycle without storing anything.
approaches.simple: Use slow and fast pointers on the sequence; if they meet somewhere other than 1, it loops.

title: Plus One
problem: A large non-negative integer is given as an array of digits (most significant first, no leading zeros). Add one to it and return the resulting digit array.
intuition: Do what you'd do on paper: add 1 to the last digit. If it becomes 10, write 0 and carry 1 left. The carry only keeps moving while digits are 9. As soon as a digit is less than 9, increment it and you are done. The only case that grows the array is all nines (999 → 1000): the answer is 1 followed by zeros.
Don't convert to an int / long: the array can have up to 100 digits.
notes: Say it like this: "I simulate adding one from the last digit. Any digit below 9 absorbs the carry and I return immediately; nines become zero and the carry moves left. If every digit was 9, I return a new array with a leading 1. That's O(n) worst case, O(1) extra space."
Common mistakes: converting to a number (overflow for long arrays); forgetting the all-9s growth case.
Follow-ups: "Add two digit arrays / Add Strings?" → same carry loop from the right over both arrays. 9.17
simple: Add 1 to a number stored as a list of digits.

approaches.label: Brute Force (general addition with carry into a new array)
steps: Create res of size n + 1, carry = 1.
From the right, sum = digits[i] + carry, write sum % 10 to res[i+1], carry = sum / 10.
Put carry in res[0]; strip the leading zero if carry == 0.
approaches.why: Always processes every digit and always allocates a new array even when only the last digit changes.
approaches.simple: Do normal addition with a carry into a new array.

approaches.label: Optimal (in place, stop at the first non-9)
steps: From the right: if digits[i] < 9, increment and return digits.
Otherwise set it to 0 and continue.
If the loop ends, every digit was 9: return a new array [1, 0, 0, …] of size n + 1.
approaches.why: We stop at the first digit that can absorb the carry; a new array is needed only when the length grows.
approaches.simple: From the right, turn 9s into 0s until you can just add 1 to a digit; if all were 9, put a 1 in front.

title: Pow(x, n)
problem: Implement pow(x, n), which computes x raised to the power n, where x is a double and n is a 32-bit signed integer (it can be negative).
example: Explanation: 2^10 = 1024. For n = -2, the answer would be 1/2^2 = 0.25.
intuition: Multiplying x by itself n times is O(n), and n can be about 2 billion. The key identity is squaring: x^n = (x^(n/2))² when n is even, and x · x^(n-1) when odd. Each step halves n, so it takes O(log n) multiplications.
Iteratively, read n in binary: x^13 = x^8 · x^4 · x^1 because 13 = 1101₂. Keep squaring a base (x, x², x⁴, x⁸, …) and multiply it into the answer whenever the current bit of n is 1.
Negative n: compute (1/x)^(-n). Careful: -Integer.MIN_VALUE overflows an int, so convert n to long first.
notes: Say it like this: "Multiplying n times is O(n). Using x^n = (x^(n/2))², I square the base and halve the exponent each step, multiplying into the result when the current bit is 1, which is O(log n) time and O(1) space. For negative n I invert x, and I store n in a long to handle Integer.MIN_VALUE."
Edge cases: n = 0 → 1; n = Integer.MIN_VALUE; x = 0 with negative n (Infinity; LeetCode avoids it); x = 1 or -1.
Common mistakes: n = -n on an int (overflow); in JS, using N >>= 1 when N = 2^31 (32-bit signed ops turn it negative).

Follow-ups: "Modular exponentiation (a^b mod m)?" → same loop with % m after every multiplication, using long. "Recursive version?" → half = pow(x, n/2); return n even? half*half: half*half*x, O(log n) stack. 9.18
simple: Compute x to the power n.

approaches.label: Brute Force (repeated multiplication)
steps: Convert n to long N; if negative, set x = 1/x, N = -N.
Multiply the result by x, N times.
approaches.why: One multiplication per unit of the exponent; times out for large n on LeetCode.
approaches.simple: Multiply x by itself n times.

approaches.label: Optimal (iterative binary exponentiation)
steps: long N = n; if negative, x = 1/x, N = -N.
While N > 0: if N is odd, res *= x. Then x *= x and N >>= 1.
approaches.why: Each loop iteration halves N, and there are no recursive calls.
approaches.simple: Square x and halve n each step, multiplying into the answer when n is odd. Only about log n steps.

title: Multiply Strings
problem: Given two non-negative integers num1 and num2 as strings, return their product as a string. You may not use big- integer libraries or convert the inputs directly to integers (they can be up to 200 digits).
intuition: Grade-school multiplication, but organised by position. If num1 has m digits and num2 has n, the product has at most m + n digits. The digit num1[i] × num2[j] (indices from the left) contributes to positions i + j and i + j + 1 of the result array: the units part goes to i + j + 1, the carry to i + j.
So allocate int[m + n], loop over every pair from the right, add the product into pos[i+j+1], then push the overflow into pos[i+j]. At the end skip leading zeros. No string additions needed.
notes: Say it like this: "The school method multiplies by each digit and adds shifted partial products as strings, which works but creates lots of intermediate strings. Instead I use an array of size m+n: digit i of num1 times digit j of num2 goes into positions i+j+1 with the carry into i+j. That's O(m·n) time and O(m+n) space with no string additions."
Edge cases: either input is "0" → "0" (not "000"); single digits; results with a carry into the top position ("99" × "99" = "9801").
Common mistakes: not stripping leading zeros; putting the carry in the wrong index; trying Long.parseLong (overflow).
Follow-ups: "Faster for huge numbers?" → Karatsuba O(n^1.585) or FFT O(n log n); mention only, rarely coded. 9.19
simple: Multiply two big numbers given as strings.

approaches.label: Brute Force (school method: multiply
approaches.lead: 1 by each digit, then add strings)
steps: For each digit of num2 from the right, multiply num1 by that single digit to get a partial product string, and append the right number of zeros.
Add the partial product to a running total using string addition.
approaches.why: There are n partial products; each is built in O(m) and added in O(m + n). Many intermediate strings are created.
approaches.simple: School method: multiply by one digit at a time and add the partial results.

approaches.label: Optimal (position array)
steps: pos = new int[m + n].
For i from m-1 down to 0, for j from n-1 down to 0: sum = d1 * d2 + pos[i+j+1]; set pos[i+j+1] = sum % 10; pos[i+j] += sum / 10.
Build the string from pos, skipping leading zeros (return "0" if nothing is left).
approaches.why: Every digit pair is multiplied once with O(1) work; the result array has m + n slots.
approaches.simple: Digit i times digit j lands in position i + j + 1 of the answer; add all products there and carry.

title: Detect Squares
problem: Design a structure that supports: - add(point): add a point [x, y] to the stream (duplicates allowed and counted separately). - count(point): given a query point, return how many ways you can choose three stored points that, together with the query point, form an axis-aligned square with positive area.
example: Explanation: (3,10),(11,2),(3,2) + query (11,10) form one square. After adding (11,2) again,
there are two choices for that corner, so the answer is 2.
intuition: An axis-aligned square is fixed by two diagonal corners. Given the query (qx, qy), if we pick a stored point (px, py) as the opposite corner, it must satisfy |px - qx| == |py - qy|!= 0. Then the other two corners are forced: (qx, py) and (px, qy). The number of squares for that diagonal is count(px,py) × count(qx,py) × count(px,qy) (multiplying because duplicates are separate choices).
So we just need a hash map from point to its count, and for each query we loop over the distinct stored points as diagonal candidates and do two O(1) lookups.
notes: Say it like this: "A square is determined by the query point and its diagonal opposite. I keep a hash map of point counts; for a query I loop over distinct stored points that lie on a diagonal (equal non-zero |dx| and |dy|) and multiply the counts of the diagonal point and the two forced corners. Add is O(1), count is O(distinct points)."
Edge cases: duplicate points (must multiply counts); the query point itself stored (excluded because dx = 0); zero- area squares (excluded).
Common mistakes: forgetting px!= qx (zero-area squares); adding instead of multiplying counts; using a list of points instead of counts.

Follow-ups: "Faster count?" → index points by x-coordinate: for each stored y on the query's column (x == qx), side d = y - qy, check both qx ± d; that is O(points in the column). "Non-axis-aligned squares?" → for each pair as one side, compute the other two corners by rotating the vector by 90°. 9.20
simple: Add points and count axis-aligned squares that use a query point as a corner.

approaches.label: Brute Force (store a list, scan for every corner)
steps: add: append the point to a list.
count: for each stored point p that is a valid diagonal, scan the whole list to count points equal to (qx, py) and (px, qy); add their product.
approaches.why: Each of N candidate diagonals triggers a full O(N) scan for the other two corners.
approaches.simple: Store every point in a list and scan for matching corners.

title: Print all primes till N
problem: Given an integer N, return all prime numbers less than or equal to N in increasing order. (GFG: "Sieve of Eratosthenes". The LeetCode cousin is "Count Primes", which counts primes strictly less than n.)
example: Explanation: 4, 6, 8, 9, 10 have divisors other than 1 and themselves; 1 is not prime.
intuition: Testing each number on its own is wasteful: you keep re-discovering that multiples of 2, 3, 5… are composite. Flip it around: once you know p is prime, cross out all its multiples at once. Any number that is never crossed out is prime.

Two refinements make it fast: start crossing at p*p (smaller multiples like 2p, 3p were already crossed by smaller primes), and stop the outer loop once p*p > N. The total work is N/2 + N/3 + N/5 + … which sums to O(N log log N), effectively linear.
notes: Say it like this: "Trial division tests each number up to its square root, O(N√N). The Sieve of Eratosthenes instead crosses out multiples of each prime starting from p², and stops once p² > N, giving O(N log log N) time and O(N) space."
Edge cases: N < 2 → empty list; N = 2 → [2]; N itself prime (include it, since the range is inclusive).

Common mistakes: treating 1 as prime; starting the inner loop at 2p (correct but slower) or at p (marks the prime itself); p * p overflow for N near Integer.MAX_VALUE; off-by-one between "≤ N" (GFG) and "< n" (LeetCode Count Primes).

Follow-ups: "Many queries for primality / factorisation?" → smallest-prime-factor sieve, then factorise any number ≤ N in O(log N). "Primes in a range [L, R] with large R?" → segmented sieve using primes up to √R.
simple: List all primes up to N.

approaches.label: Brute Force (trial division up to √i)
steps: For each i from 2 to N, check divisibility by every d with d*d <= i.
If none divides, i is prime.
approaches.why: Each of N numbers is tested with up to √N divisions.
approaches.simple: Check each number by trying divisors up to its square root.

approaches.label: Optimal (Sieve of Eratosthenes)
steps: composite = new boolean[N + 1].
For p from 2 while p*p <= N: if p is not composite, mark p*p, p*p + p, …, ≤ N as composite.
Collect every i in [2, N] that is not composite.
approaches.why: Each prime p crosses out about N/p numbers, and the sum of 1/p over primes up to N grows like log log N.
approaches.simple: Sieve: cross out multiples of each prime; what is left uncrossed is prime.
